findings.reason: The protected Python solution counts character frequencies with Counter(s), sorts the frequencies descending, and multiplies position i's frequency by (i // 9 + 1). Assigning highest frequencies to cheap key positions (1st 9 get cost 1, 2nd 9 get cost 2, last 8 get cost 3) is optimal and concise; no candidate is required.
By the exchange argument, pairing descending character frequencies with ascending slot press costs (1 for first 9 letters, 2 for next 9, 3 for last 8) minimizes total keypresses.

Counting s of length n takes O(n) time. Sorting 26 frequencies takes O(26 log 26) = O(1) time. Total time complexity is O(n) with O(1) auxiliary space for 26 alphabet counters. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts a lowercase string s and returns the minimum total keypresses across all valid 26-letter assignments to 9 buttons.

The approach accurately details multiset slot costs, greedy descending frequency pairing proof, and O(n) time / O(1) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover testing layouts, recounting per position, alphabetical assignment, 1..9 used letters, 10..18 used letters, 26 used letters, tied frequencies, absent letters, and single-letter strings.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the exact same greedy frequency counting algorithm with SHA-256 digests 4344f118126439645882001bf52621227f7fc67b7e1c2fe4d74223cff5ff360a and a15811d89929b94445dd1c70faed341539be61001edcfdf1ecc6efa52f6c49f2. Verified submission remains untouched.
